prompt:
A simulated brick world had this hidden rule:
In this world the agent's observation shows the target shifted: the target, missing, extra and target-height channels are rolled 4 columns toward higher x, wrapping around. The world, its designs and scoring are as described.

Below is what an AI scientist wrote during a search in that world: its analysis at every round, in order, and the
name and hypothesis of the trial it ended with. Does the text, anywhere, state the rule?
- "yes": it states the rule's substance (what is changed and how).
- "partly": it identifies the right kind of change but not its specifics.
- "no": anything else.

## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
No trials have run yet. The starting architecture learned to choose DONE at the first step on both seeds. The trace suggests why. The target, as observed, is the real design shifted cyclically by X/2 = 4 columns: design row 1 '00220000' appears as '00000022', and diagnostic design 2 shows the same shift. Rewards and actions use the unshifted design. The baseline's receptive field is only 5x5, so it cannot see the target cell that matches a placement. Placements then look negative on average, and DONE (reward 0) takes over. I propose two fixes. The first gives the network cyclically shifted copies of the observation, built only by slicing and concatenating, and tests it with the default recipe and with a recipe that updates more often. The second uses learned mixing along whole rows and whole columns, which makes no assumption about the size of the shift. If all three score 0, the shift is not the main problem, and DONE collapse or exploration needs attention.

### Round 2
The x-shift theory is confirmed: targets look cyclically shifted by X/2 in x. Without the shifted copy a network scores 0, and learned row/column mixing (r1c2) learned almost nothing. With the copy, r1c1 scored 0.59 (seeds 0.48 and 0.70). r1c3 used the same network with about 83 updates instead of about 30 and scored 0.53 (seeds 0.91 and 0.16). Its seed 0 reached 0.857 training success against 0.433 for r1c1, so the number of updates and samples is a main limit. The 0.16 seed is likely a slow start that stalls as the learning rate decays to 0. Seed spread is about ±0.4, so only large or consistent gains count. Runs take about 60 of the 900 seconds allowed, so time is not a constraint, but a bigger network means fewer samples. This round keeps the r1c3 setup and changes one thing each: fewer epochs for more samples, more and smaller updates, and a skip path that gives the head the exact per-cell layer features.

### Round 3
The half-width shifted copy of obs was the key fix. The target channels are misaligned with action coordinates, and once a copy aligned them, learning started. Learned row/column mixing did not find the misalignment (0.02). On the recipe side, cutting PPO epochs from 3 to 2 helped a lot: on the same network, r1c3 scored 0.53 with high variance and r2c1 scored 0.92 with both seeds above 0.9. More samples matter on this small budget. The collapse in r2c2 (64 envs with minibatches of 256, every episode ending in DONE on both seeds) suggests that small, noisy batches early on push the agent towards DONE. Adding the stem skip into the footprint head (r2c3) gave the best result, 0.94 at 3 epochs, with both seeds consistent. That network has not been tried with 2 epochs, so that is the obvious combination. Dev IoU is about 0.99, so the remaining failures are small errors: overhang or ordering mistakes, or stopping early.

### Round 4
An x-shifted copy of the observation fixed a fixed X/2 misalignment between target channels and action coordinates (0 → 0.59). The stem-feature skip into the footprint head gave the best result (r2c3, 0.94). Recipe: 128 envs with 2–3 epochs beat the default, and batches of 1,024 collapsed to DONE. Runs are fragile: single seeds fell to 0.15 (r1c3, r3c1) and 0.45 (r3c2), so 2 vs 3 epochs is within noise. The weak r3c1 seed stopped too early (IoU 0.83, almost no cells outside the target, training success flat near 0.2); the weak r3c3 seed placed wrong cells. My guess: the DONE and value heads see only pooled post-3x3 features and do not reliably know whether target cells are still missing. Giving them pooled per-cell stem features (which carry missing/extra cells directly) should make stopping reliable and improve the critic. All three candidates add this, each with a different recipe.

## Trial it ended with
name: stem-pooled done/value, 3 epochs
hypothesis: The r2c3 network and recipe, but the DONE and value heads also get the mean and max over cells of the 1x1 stem features. These carry the aligned missing/extra cells for each layer, so 'any target cell still missing?' becomes nearly linear. That should stop early DONE and improve the critic. Refuted if the mean is not above 0.94 or a seed falls below 0.85.

Return a JSON object: "verdict" ("yes", "partly" or "no") and "evidence" (at most 80 words, quoting the text and
naming the round it comes from).
